passages.happening:
After Ehud dies, Israel does evil again. The LORD sells them into the hand of Jabin, ‘king of Canaan, who reigned in Hazor’. His commander is Sisera (verse 2). Jabin has nine hundred chariots of iron, and he oppresses Israel harshly for twenty years, until they cry out to the LORD (verse 3).

“Now Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lappidoth, was judging Israel at that time” (verse 4). She sits under a palm tree between Ramah and Bethel, and the people come up to her to settle their disputes (verse 5).

She sends for Barak, from Kedesh in the north, and gives him God's command: go to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun, and God will draw Sisera and his chariots to the River Kishon and give him into Barak's hand (verses 6-7).

Barak answers, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go” (verse 8). Deborah agrees, with a warning: “the road you are taking will bring you no honor, because the LORD will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman” (verse 9). She goes with him, and ten thousand men follow (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
This time the enemy comes from inside the land. Jabin is a Canaanite king in the north, the kind of power chapter 1 said the tribes had failed to drive out. Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city in Canaan. The book of Joshua says that Joshua burned Hazor and killed its king, also called Jabin, and how the two accounts fit together is debated. Some think Jabin was a name used by more than one king and that Hazor recovered for a time. Others think both books tell the same events from different traditions. Others see a later ruler of a rebuilt city. The book calls him king of Canaan, which suggests the leader of an alliance of northern cities.

Chariots were the advanced weapon of the age, fast and terrifying on flat, dry ground. Nine hundred of them was a fearsome number for farmers who fought on foot.

Deborah is both a prophetess and a judge. A prophetess speaks the word of God. She is one of only a few women in the Old Testament given that title, beside Miriam before her and Huldah after her. Her ‘judgment’ means that she decided disputes, the one judge in the book shown doing that work. Her authority to summon Barak rests on the word of God she speaks, not on any military rank. The words ‘the wife of Lappidoth’ can also be read as woman of torches, since lappidoth means torches, though most translations take it as her husband's name. Barak's own name means lightning.

Barak's answer has been read in more than one way. Some hear weak faith, a man who would not trust God's word without the prophet at his side. Others hear a right instinct, a man who wanted the word of God with him in the battle. Many hear something of both. What is clear is Deborah's answer. The honor of the victory will not be his. It will go to a woman, and a first-time reader expects that woman to be Deborah.
passages.later:
Deborah stands in a short line of women the Bible calls prophetess: “Then Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, took a tambourine in her hand” (Exodus 15:20), and centuries later the king's officials ‘spoke to Huldah the prophetess’ (2 Kings 22:14).

The book of Joshua tells of an earlier king of Hazor named Jabin: “At that time Joshua turned back and captured Hazor and put its king to the sword, because Hazor was formerly the head of all these kingdoms” (Joshua 11:10).

The letter to the Hebrews names Barak among those who acted by faith: “Time will not allow me to tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah” (Hebrews 11:32).
passages.asks: Barak would not go without the word of God at his side. Ask what you need before you will do what God has asked of you, and whether that need is faith or fear. And notice that the honor went to someone else. Ask whether you would still obey God if someone else received the credit.

passages.happening:
A short note introduces a family that will matter. Heber the Kenite has moved away from the rest of his clan and pitched his tent near Kedesh (verse 11).

Sisera hears that Barak has gone up Mount Tabor. He gathers all nine hundred iron chariots and his army at the River Kishon (verses 12-13).

Deborah tells Barak, “Arise, for this is the day that the LORD has delivered Sisera into your hand. Has not the LORD gone before you?” (verse 14). Barak comes down the mountain with his ten thousand.

“And in front of him the LORD routed with the sword Sisera, all his charioteers, and all his army. Sisera abandoned his chariot and fled on foot” (verse 15). Barak pursues the chariots and the army, and not a man of Sisera's army is left (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The battle took place in the Jezreel Valley, the broad plain between Galilee and the hills of Samaria, drained by the River Kishon. Mount Tabor is a rounded hill rising steeply from that plain. On its slopes Barak's men on foot were out of reach of the chariots.

Then they came down, and the chariots should have crushed them. Instead, the LORD ‘routed’ Sisera. The Hebrew word means to throw into confusion or panic, and it is the word used of what God did to Pharaoh's chariots at the Red Sea. The writer is telling the story as a new exodus. The song in the next chapter adds that the Kishon swept the enemy away, which suggests that a sudden storm turned the plain to mud and made the chariots useless.

The greatest weapon of the age ends stuck in a valley, and its commander runs on foot. The thing Israel feared most proves powerless before God.

Deborah's question, ‘Has not the LORD gone before you?’, is the heart of the scene. The battle was won before it was fought.

The Kenites were a clan related to Moses' family by marriage. Heber had separated from them and, as verse 17 will say, made peace with Jabin. The writer places his tent on the map just before Sisera needs somewhere to run.
passages.later:
The words for the rout echo the Red Sea: “the LORD looked down on the army of the Egyptians from the pillar of fire and cloud, and He threw their camp into confusion. He caused their chariot wheels to wobble” (Exodus 14:24-25).

A psalm puts the lesson in one line: “Some trust in chariots and others in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7). Another prays for God to act again ‘as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon’ (Psalm 83:9).
passages.asks: Nine hundred iron chariots were the measure of Israel's fear for twenty years. Ask what has been the measure of your fear, the thing that seems too strong to face. Hear Deborah's question, ‘Has not the LORD gone before you?’ Ask where you need to come down from the safe high ground and trust that he has.

passages.happening:
Sisera runs on foot to the tent of Jael, the wife of Heber the Kenite, ‘because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite’ (verse 17).

Jael comes out to meet him. “Come in, my lord. Come in with me. Do not be afraid” (verse 18). He goes in, and she covers him with a blanket. He asks for water, and she gives him milk and covers him again (verse 19). He tells her to stand at the door and, if anyone asks whether a man is inside, to say no (verse 20).

While he sleeps, exhausted, Jael takes a tent peg and a hammer, goes to him quietly, and drives the peg through his temple, and he dies (verse 21).

Barak arrives in pursuit, and Jael goes out to meet him: “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking” (verse 22). Sisera lies dead in her tent.

“On that day God subdued Jabin king of Canaan before the Israelites” (verse 23), and Israel grows stronger against him until he is destroyed (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
Deborah's word comes true, but not as a reader expected. The woman into whose hand the LORD sells Sisera is not Deborah. It is Jael, a woman of a family that was not part of Israel and had made peace with Israel's enemy.

In the ancient Near East, hospitality was a sacred duty. A guest in one's tent was under one's protection. It was also true that a woman's tent was her own place, which no man but her husband would normally enter. Sisera breaks that custom by hiding there, and he asks her to lie for him. Jael breaks the duty to a guest. Both of them do what was not expected.

Setting up and taking down tents was usually women's work among people who lived in tents, so Jael knew how to use a peg and a hammer.

The writer slows down in the tent: the welcome, the blanket, the milk, the order to lie, the sleep, the peg. There is irony in Sisera's last order. He tells her to say there is no man inside. By the end, that is true. The great commander has become nothing.

The writer then gives the credit where it belongs. It was ‘God’ who subdued Jabin that day. Not Barak, not Deborah, not Jael.
passages.later:
Samuel later named this oppression among those from which God rescued Israel: “He sold them into the hand of Sisera the commander of the army of Hazor” (1 Samuel 12:9).

The next chapter tells the same story again as a song, and it calls Jael “Most blessed among women” (Judges 5:24). Luke's Gospel echoes those words when Elizabeth greets Mary (Luke 1:42), as the note on chapter 5 explains.
passages.hard:
Is Jael a hero or a murderer, and why does the song praise her?

Jael welcomed Sisera, told him not to be afraid, gave him milk, and killed him while he slept. That broke the sacred trust owed to a guest, and it broke her household's peace with Jabin. And the song in chapter 5 says of her, “Most blessed among women is Jael” (5:24).

Readers have weighed her act in more than one way. Some defend her as acting in a war against a brutal enemy commander who had crushed Israel for twenty years, choosing the side of God's people at great risk to herself. Others stress that Scripture records her act, and that the song celebrates Israel's rescue, without passing a full moral judgment on the way it was done. Still others note that Sisera himself broke custom when he entered a woman's tent, and that he asked her to lie.

Readers across these views agree on one thing. The text presents Sisera's death as the outworking of God's word in verse 9. It leaves the rights and wrongs of the act for the reader to weigh, and these notes do not force an answer.

On any reading this is a story of a war long ago. It is no pattern for anyone today, and it gives no one a warrant to deceive or harm a person who has trusted them.
passages.asks: God's word came true through someone no one expected, an outsider in a tent. Ask whom you have overlooked because they did not seem to belong to God's story. Then sit with the hard part. Ask how you weigh an act that rescued many and broke a trust, and why your answer matters for how you treat the people who trust you.
